title: Mindfulness everywhere
hookLine: meditation in hospitals, schools and offices: what it gives, and what can be lost when ethics are left out

lines: A MINDFUL MINUTE ON YOUR PHONE.
WHAT CAME ALONG, WHAT WAS LEFT?
cards: A phone buzzes mid-afternoon: time for a mindful minute. A nurse on a break sits in a quiet room with an audio track. A class of children puts their hands on their bellies and counts breaths before a test.
An office books meditation between budget meetings. A practice that grew up in monasteries now turns up in hospitals, schools and offices, without robes, bells or Buddhist words.
A fair question: what does it bring with it, and what might it leave behind?

teach.b: The Pali word usually translated as mindfulness is sati.
In the Buddha's teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, it means steady, clear awareness of the body, of feelings, of the mind, and of how things arise and pass.
Teachers in hospitals and clinics offered practices like these without religious language, to help people living with pain, stress and illness.
Some people say it has helped them, and researchers have studied it, which is tomorrow's story.

Supporters, including some Buddhist teachers, see a door opened wide: people who would never walk into a temple can still learn to sit with their breath. And some programs do teach kindness alongside attention.
But some Buddhist teachers and scholars have raised a worry. In the path as the old texts lay it out, mindfulness doesn't stand alone.
Right mindfulness is one part of the path, alongside right speech, action and livelihood, right intention and right effort.
Attention by itself is a tool, and a tool can serve anything; you can be very focused while doing something harmful.
In the path, sati is held inside sila, ethical conduct, and inside compassion, so what you notice turns into how you treat people. Both sides want the same good thing: less suffering.

One says start where people are, and the rest may follow. The other says keep the whole path in view, or the practice can be bent to other ends. Today's line holds both: the breath at your desk, and the ethics around it.

how: In Buddhist settings, mindfulness is taught alongside the precepts, loving-kindness and the rest of the path; in secular programs, it's taught as attention training, and some programs add kindness practices.

games.q: keep the ethics: tap the pairs.

games.q: a company wants a meditation course to make staff more focused. a Buddhist teacher is asked to lead it. what's the teacher's worry, in today's lesson?
o: that meditation doesn't work outside temples
that attention without ethics is a tool that can serve anything
that the course is too short
games.why: in the Buddha's path, sati sits inside sila and compassion; on its own, attention can be bent to other ends.

practice: Feel the breath, in at the nose, the belly rising and falling, and when the mind wanders, notice and come back.
Then, without dropping the breath, bring to mind someone you'll see later today, and with each out-breath let a wish go to them: may your day go well. Attention, with kindness riding on it.

wordCard.voice: Mindfulness everywhere. Sati carried into hospitals, schools and offices, with the question of whether the ethics travel with it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sati: the word usually translated as mindfulness, steady clear awareness.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the ethics. Sati, held inside sila and inside compassion, too. See you tomorrow.
